meta.title: Who really said "When a man is at peace with his gods and ancestors, his harvest will be good or bad according to the strength of his arm"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Real Achebe, but not his maxim: the priestess Chika says it in Things Fall Apart (1958), ch. 3. The novel reads "his gods and his ancestors."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When a man is at peace with his gods and ancestors, his harvest will be good or bad according to the strength of his arm'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified in Things Fall Apart, chapter 3 — but it's the priestess Chika's rebuke to Unoka, not Achebe speaking, and the real text has one more word.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and traceable to the page: the sentence appears in Things Fall Apart (Heinemann, 1958), chapter 3. Two honest caveats, though — it is spoken by a character, the priestess Chika, rebuking Okonkwo’s feckless father Unoka, rather than by Achebe in his own voice; and the novel actually reads “his gods and his ancestors.” The circulating version quietly drops that second “his.”

source.excerpt: You have offended neither the gods nor your fathers. And when a man is at peace with his gods and his ancestors, his harvest will be good or bad according to the strength of his arm.
trail: The line is genuine and locatable, which is not the usual outcome for a famous name. It sits in chapter 3 of Things Fall Apart, Achebe’s 1958 debut, first published in London by Heinemann on 17 June 1958 ↗.

Read against the novel’s own text, the passage runs “when a man is at peace with his gods and his ancestors” — one word more than the version in circulation. It is the priestess Chika’s answer to Unoka, who has just finished listing every sacrifice he makes and is about to accuse the gods of shorting him.
The trimmed wording, stripped of speaker and chapter and filed under the author’s name, is the form Goodreads carries ↗; from there it spread to the quote-aggregator ecosystem largely unchanged.

Notably, Wikiquote’s Achebe page ↗ does not list the line at all, and Quote Investigator has never examined it — there was no attribution dispute to settle, only a slow accretion of small errors around a real sentence.
source.excerptNote: Quoted only as far as the verification requires, since the novel remains in copyright. Chika’s speech continues past this point: she tells Unoka he is known throughout the clan for the weakness of his machete and his hoe, that he sows on exhausted farms while his neighbours cross seven rivers and cut down virgin forest, and she dismisses him with an instruction to go home and work like a man.

author.name: Chinua Achebe
author.heading: Who was Chinua Achebe?
author.bio: Born in Ogidi in colonial Nigeria in 1930, Achebe wrote Things Fall Apart as his debut novel at twenty-seven; it became the most widely read, studied and translated African novel ever written. He is routinely called the father of modern African literature — a label he rejected — for writing Igbo life from the inside, in English, against a century of European caricature. He went on to complete the African Trilogy with No Longer at Ease (1960) and Arrow of God (1964), and died in Boston in 2013.

misattribution.heading: What the internet gets wrong
misattribution.intro: This one is not a fabrication — the sentence is really Achebe’s prose, in a real book, in a findable chapter. But almost every site that quotes it distorts it in one of three ways, and the errors have been copied from each other for years.

items.why: The novel reads “his gods and his ancestors.” A small drop, but it flattens the parallel Achebe built — two separate reckonings, gods and ancestors, each owed peace in its own right. The trimmed form is the one Goodreads carries ↗ and the one that propagated everywhere.

items.who: Chinua Achebe, speaking his own mind
items.why: Quote sites file it under Achebe’s name as though it were a personal aphorism. It is dialogue: the priestess of Agbala shouting down a man who came to blame the gods for his own laziness. Wikiquote’s Achebe page ↗ does not carry it at all, which is the more disciplined position.

A popular roundup that otherwise gets the chapter right — this one, for instance ↗ — names Chielo as the speaker. Both women are priestesses of Agbala, but Achebe is explicit that they are different people in different eras: Chika held the shrine “in those days,” when Okonkwo was a boy; Chielo is the priestess of the novel’s present and is not introduced until chapter 6.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is authentically Achebe’s, from chapter 3 of Things Fall Apart, published by Heinemann in June 1958 ↗ — but it belongs in the mouth of Chika, the priestess who tells a lazy man that his gods are not the ones failing him.

context.heading: Why the line lands
lead: The scene is a small masterpiece of misdirection. Unoka — Okonkwo’s father, a flute-playing debtor with no talent for work — crawls into the shrine of Agbala to ask why his crops keep failing. He recites his piety like an invoice: a cock to Ani, a cock at the shrine of Ifejioku, the bush cleared, the yams staked. He is building to a grievance against the gods.

The priestess cuts him off before he can finish. He has offended nobody, she tells him; that is precisely the problem. Once the ledger with the gods and the ancestors is square, nothing stands between a man and his harvest except his own arm — and Unoka is known throughout the clan for the weakness of his machete and his hoe. The sentence is not consolation. It is the door closing on his last excuse.
context.detailsSummary: The line’s job in the novel
detailsBody: Achebe puts this speech many years in the past, when Okonkwo was still a boy, and it explains the whole man Okonkwo becomes. Okonkwo’s ferocious industry, his contempt for gentleness, his terror of resembling his father — all of it grows from watching Unoka be told, by the voice of the god itself, that he had only himself to blame.

It is also Achebe doing quiet cultural argument. A European reader arriving with assumptions about fatalistic “natives” ruled by superstition meets an Igbo theology that hands responsibility straight back to the individual. The gods must be kept at peace; after that, the harvest is a matter of labour.
context.pull: Piety settles the account with the gods. It does not clear the bush.
